title: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
summary: Why proxies, CDNs and caches read the same request differently: CL.TE, TE.CL, HTTP/2 downgrades, client-side desync, cache poisoning and cache deception, with toy parsers and the fixes.
outcomes: Explain how HTTP/1.1 frames a body with Content-Length or chunked coding, and why both together are ambiguous
Trace CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE, CL.0 and 0.CL desyncs through two toy parsers and say which side reads fewer bytes
Explain why HTTP/2 end to end removes framing ambiguity and which RFC 9113 checks a downgrading proxy must make
Configure strict parsing, connection closing and upstream HTTP/2, and read ALB desync classification logs
Explain cache keys, Vary and Cache-Control, and how unkeyed inputs and cached errors poison a shared cache
Explain web cache deception and path confusion, and fix them with origin Cache-Control and allow-list caching
Detect desync and cache incidents by comparing tiers, and respond by containing, purging and revoking

lessons.title: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree

blocks.md:
Imagine two clerks reading the same stack of forms. One clerk thinks a form ends at the line "total pages: 2"; the other thinks it ends at the first blank page. Hand them a form with both, and they will disagree about where the *next* form starts. Everything in this course is that disagreement, applied to HTTP.

A modern web request rarely goes straight to the application. It passes a **CDN** (content delivery network: servers spread around the world that answer from nearby copies), a **load balancer** (spreads requests across many app servers) and finally the **origin** (the server that really owns the content). Anything that receives a request and forwards it is an **intermediary**; the one nearest the user is the **front end**, the one behind it the **back end**.

Two facts make intermediaries dangerous. First, HTTP/1.1 uses **persistent connections** (also called keep-alive): RFC 9112, the HTTP/1.1 standard, makes it the default to carry many requests and responses over one TCP connection. Second, front ends reuse their connections to the back end for requests from *different users*, because opening a fresh connection for each request is slow.

So the back end receives one long stream of bytes, containing Ana's request, then Ben's, then Chen's, and must cut it into messages exactly where the front end did. If the two cut in different places, a piece of one user's request becomes the start of another's. You met this idea in the prerequisite lesson *When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon*; this course takes it apart byte by byte.

blocks.title: Many users, one reused back-end connection

scenes.caption: Each browser has its own connection to the CDN edge. Behind the edge, one connection to the origin is shared.
Ana's request arrives first and is forwarded on the shared connection.
Ben's request follows on the same connection. The origin must find the exact byte where Ana's request ended and Ben's began.
The edge also keeps a cache. It must decide which stored response belongs to which request: a second place where two components can disagree.

blocks.md:
The course follows two families of bugs:

1. **Boundary disagreements**: front end and back end split the byte stream differently. This is **HTTP request smuggling** (the attacker smuggles a partial request inside their own), also called an **HTTP desync attack** (short for desynchronisation: the two servers fall out of step). The Common Weakness Enumeration lists the class as CWE-444, *Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests*.
2. **Identity disagreements**: a cache and the origin disagree about which requests are "the same". That gives **web cache poisoning** (a harmful response is stored and served to everyone) and **web cache deception** (a private response is stored where the attacker can fetch it).

For every bug you will see two toy parsers written in Python that read the same bytes differently, then the fix next to them.

Every bug in this course is a **parser differential**: two programs read the same message and reach different conclusions. The durable fixes remove the room for disagreement (one unambiguous framing, one definition of the cache key) rather than trying to spot bad requests one by one.

Testing a site's proxies or cache for these bugs can harm *other* users, because the leftover bytes or poisoned entries land on real people. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test, and prefer your own lab: the toys in this course run entirely in one Python process.

blocks.question: Why does connection reuse between a front end and a back end matter for request smuggling?
options: It makes TLS weaker on the back-end hop
Requests from different users travel on one byte stream, so a boundary error moves bytes from one user's request into another's
It doubles the number of requests the back end must handle
It stops the back end from reading headers
blocks.explain: Reuse is what puts several users' requests on the same stream. If each request had its own connection, leftover bytes would only ever affect the sender. TLS strength and request volume are unrelated to the boundary problem.

lessons.title: Where an HTTP/1.1 message ends: Content-Length and chunked

blocks.md:
**Framing** means deciding where a message starts and stops. An HTTP/1.1 request is text: a request line (`POST /notes HTTP/1.1`), header fields one per line, an empty line, then an optional body. Lines end with **CRLF** (carriage return plus line feed, the two control bytes 0x0D and 0x0A), written `\r\n` in code.

The header section always ends at the first empty line. The body is the hard part, and RFC 9112 section 6.3 gives the rules in order of precedence. For requests: if a **Transfer-Encoding** field is present and **chunked** is the final coding, read chunks; otherwise, if a valid **Content-Length** is present, read exactly that many bytes; otherwise the body is empty.

**Content-Length** is a decimal count of body bytes. `Content-Length: 11` followed by `hello world` is complete after 11 bytes.

**Chunked** transfer coding exists for senders who do not know the size in advance, such as a server streaming a generated page. The body is sent as a series of chunks: each starts with its size in **hexadecimal** (base 16), a CRLF, the data, and another CRLF. A chunk of size zero, then an empty line, ends the body. The name says what it does: the content is cut into chunks, each with its own size.

blocks.title: Decoding a chunked body, chunk by chunk

scenes.caption: 26 bytes arrive after the headers. The parser reads a size line first: 5 in hexadecimal is 5 bytes.
It copies exactly 5 bytes, hello, then expects a CRLF after the data.
The next size line says 6. The 6 bytes are a space plus world.
A size of 0 means the last chunk. An empty line (the final CRLF) closes the body: 11 content bytes travelled in 26 bytes on the wire, 15 of them framing.

blocks.md:
Now the rule that matters for this course. A request can carry **both** headers. RFC 9112 says Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length, that such a message "might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling" and "ought to be handled as an error", and that an intermediary that forwards it MUST first remove Content-Length. A server MAY reject it or use Transfer-Encoding alone, and either way MUST close the connection after responding.

Why allow both at all? The RFC explains that early implementations sent chunked framing *plus* an estimated Content-Length for progress bars, so Transfer-Encoding was defined to win rather than making the pair illegal. Compatibility with old software is the root of the ambiguity.

blocks.caption: A strict request parser that follows RFC 9112 section 6.3 and rejects instead of guessing. Simplified: no trailers or chunk extensions, and the caller must close the connection after any 400.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
(b'POST /notes HTTP/1.1', b'hello world', b'')
400: both TE and CL
400: Content-Length b'+5'
400: chunk size b'0x5'
```

The parser decodes the chunked body, then rejects three messages a lenient parser would accept.

Python's own number parsing is lenient: `int('0x5', 16)` and `int('+5')` both return 5, and `int('1_0', 16)` returns 16 because underscores are allowed. That is why the parser checks that a chunk size contains only hex digits and Content-Length only decimal digits **before** converting. Two servers that both "parse numbers" can still disagree about which strings are numbers.

blocks.question: A request has `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Content-Length: 40`. Following RFC 9112, what should a server that chooses to process it do?
options: Use Content-Length, because it appears first
Use the larger of the two lengths
Use chunked framing, and close the connection after responding
blocks.explain: Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length, and the server MUST close the connection after responding so that any bytes it misjudged cannot start another request. Rejecting with 400 is the other allowed choice, and the safer one for a front end.

blocks.question: Why does the chunk-size line need its own validation, rather than just calling int(size, 16)?
options: A lenient converter accepts strings such as 0x5 that another server may reject or read differently, creating a disagreement
blocks.explain: The danger is not speed but disagreement: if one hop treats 0x5 as 5 and another rejects it or stops at the x, they now frame the body differently.

lessons.title: CL.TE and TE.CL: two parsers, one stream

blocks.md:
Researchers name a desync by which length each side believed, front end first. **CL.TE**: the front end uses Content-Length and the back end uses Transfer-Encoding. **TE.CL**: the reverse. **TE.TE**: both support Transfer-Encoding, but one can be made to ignore it (next lesson). The naming comes from the research and training material of PortSwigger, the company behind the Burp Suite web testing tool.

The idea dates to a 2005 paper, *HTTP Request Smuggling*, by Chaim Linhart, Amit Klein, Ronen Heled and Steve Orrin of Watchfire, a web security company; RFC 9112 cites it in its own section on request smuggling. Below are two deliberately sloppy toy parsers. Parser A only knows Content-Length. Parser B lets chunked win. Both are fed the same stream: a first request carrying both headers, then an ordinary second request.

blocks.code:
def headers(buf):
    head, _, rest = buf.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
    lines = head.split(b"\r\n")
    h = {}
    for l in lines[1:]:
        k, _, v = l.partition(b":")
        h[k.strip().lower()] = v.strip()
    return lines[0], h, rest

def by_length(buf):        # toy parser A: only reads Content-Length
    line, h, rest = headers(buf)
    n = int(h.get(b"content-length", b"0"))
    return line, rest[:n], rest[n:]

def by_chunks(buf):        # toy parser B: chunked wins if present
    line, h, rest = headers(buf)
    if h.get(b"transfer-encoding") != b"chunked":
        n = int(h.get(b"content-length", b"0"))
        return line, rest[:n], rest[n:]
    body = b""
    while True:
        size, _, rest = rest.partition(b"\r\n")
        n = int(size, 16)
        if n == 0:
            return line, body, rest[2:]
        body, rest = body + rest[:n], rest[n + 2:]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    first = (b"POST /a HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s.example\r\n"
             b"Content-Length: 13\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"
             b"0\r\n\r\nLEFTOVER")
    second = b"GET /home HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s.example\r\n\r\n"
    stream = first + second            # one reused connection

    for name, parse in [("A (length)", by_length), ("B (chunks)", by_chunks)]:
        line, body, rest = parse(stream)
        nxt = rest.split(b"\r\n")[0]
        print(f"{name}: body={body!r} next request line={nxt!r}")
blocks.caption: Two toy parsers on one stream. The first request's body is 13 bytes by Content-Length, but its chunked body ends after the zero-size chunk. LEFTOVER is a harmless marker, not a request.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
A (length): body=b'0\r\n\r\nLEFTOVER' next request line=b'GET /home HTTP/1.1'
B (chunks): body=b'' next request line=b'LEFTOVERGET /home HTTP/1.1'
```

Parser A swallows all 13 bytes as body, so it sees the second request start cleanly. Parser B stops at the zero-size chunk, so the 8 bytes `LEFTOVER` stay in its buffer and are glued to the front of the next request line. If A is the front end and B the back end, the back end now believes the second request, possibly another user's, begins with bytes the first sender chose.

scenes.caption: Simplified: each cell is a piece of the stream, LEFTOV stands for the 8 bytes LEFTOVER. Both parsers read the same request line and headers.
The front end trusts Content-Length 13 and counts 13 body bytes: the zero chunk, two CRLFs and LEFTOVER. It forwards everything as request 1, then forwards GET /home as request 2.
The back end trusts chunked framing. The body ends at the zero-size chunk and the empty line, so request 1 ends earlier.
LEFTOVER waits in the back end's buffer. When the next request arrives, the back end reads LEFTOVERGET /home as one request line: the boundary has moved.

blocks.prompt: Now reverse the roles (TE.CL). The first request has `Content-Length: 3` and a chunked body: a chunk of size 8 containing LEFTOVER, then the zero chunk. The front end frames by chunks, the back end by length. What does the back end think the next request starts with?
blocks.reveal:
Running the same two parsers in the other order on this stream prints:
```
front end forwards body b'LEFTOVER' then b'GET /home HTTP/1.1'
back end body b'8\r\n' then b'LEFTOVER'
```
The front end reads the whole chunked body and forwards it. The back end reads only 3 bytes (`8` and a CRLF) as the body, so its next request starts at `LEFTOVER`. Same flaw, opposite direction: whichever side reads *less* leaves bytes behind.

blocks.md: **The fix, at the parser.** The strict parser from the last lesson refuses a request carrying both headers with a 400 and the caller closes the connection, so nothing is left in any buffer. RFC 9112 requires the close even when a server chooses to process such a request using Transfer-Encoding. **The fix, in the architecture.** The front end should normalise: if it forwards a request that had both headers, it must strip Content-Length and forward clean chunked (or re-frame with a single correct Content-Length), so the back end has nothing to disagree with. And the back end should still reject anything ambiguous that reaches it, in case the front end has a bug.

A desync needs only this: one hop reads **fewer** body bytes than the hop in front of it. The bytes it did not read become the start of the next request on that connection. Reject ambiguous framing at every hop and close the connection whenever framing is in doubt.

blocks.question: In a CL.TE setup, which side leaves bytes unread?
options: The back end, because chunked framing ended before the Content-Length count
The front end, because it reads Content-Length
blocks.explain: In the toy, the front end counted 13 bytes and forwarded them all; the back end's chunked parse ended after 5. The 8 bytes it never consumed sit in its buffer and prefix the next request.

blocks.question: Which change at the back end most directly removes the CL.TE disagreement shown above?
options: Return 400 for any request that has both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length, then close the connection
blocks.explain: Rejecting the ambiguous message and closing the connection means no leftover bytes survive. Logging helps detection but changes nothing; header size and caching are unrelated to framing.

lessons.title: TE.TE and lenient parsing: when headers are spelled oddly

blocks.md:
If both servers honour Transfer-Encoding, an attacker needs one of them to *not recognise* it. That is the TE.TE variant, and it depends on **lenient parsing**: accepting malformed input and guessing what the sender meant.

Leniency has a famous motto, the **robustness principle**, which first appeared in the RFC series in the 1980 Internet Protocol specification (RFC 760), edited by Jon Postel, an early editor of Internet standards: an implementation "should be conservative in its sending behavior, and liberal in its receiving behavior." [RFC 9413](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9413.html), *Maintaining Robust Protocols* (2023, from the Internet Architecture Board), revisits it and concludes that tolerating unexpected inputs "is no longer considered best practice in all scenarios", because silently accepted faults pile up. Request smuggling is a sharp example: two liberal receivers, each liberal in its own way.

blocks.caption: Parser A trims spaces around field names and keeps the last duplicate. Parser B keeps names exactly and keeps the first duplicate. The strict function applies RFC 9112 and rejects.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
space before colon A=chunked       B=length 6      strict=400 (whitespace before colon)
two lengths        A=length 40     B=length 6      strict=400 (duplicate Content-Length)
```

With a space before the colon, A sees `Transfer-Encoding` and uses chunked framing, while B sees an unknown field named `Transfer-Encoding ` (with a trailing space) and falls back to Content-Length 6. With two Content-Length values, A uses 40 and B uses 6. Either pair of parsers would desync. The strict function rejects both messages. (It rejects any repeated Content-Length; the RFC allows a repeated field only when all values are identical.)

blocks.title: One malformed field line, three readings

nodes.label:
Field line with a space
before the colon

A: trims the name
frames by chunks

B: unknown field
frames by length 6

scenes.caption: The same header bytes reach three parsers. Simplified: real servers differ in many more ways than these two rules.
Parser A guesses the sender meant Transfer-Encoding and uses chunked framing.
Parser B treats the oddly named field as unrelated and uses Content-Length. A in front of B is a TE.CL desync; B in front of A is CL.TE.
RFC 9112 removes the guess: a server MUST reject a request with whitespace between a field name and the colon. Nothing is left to disagree about.

blocks.md: RFC 9112 closes many of these doors explicitly. A server **MUST** reject (400) whitespace between a field name and the colon, noting that differences here "have led to security vulnerabilities". **Obsolete line folding** (continuing a field value on the next line by starting it with a space, called obs-fold) MUST be rejected or replaced with spaces before forwarding. A **bare CR** (a carriage return without a line feed) MUST be treated as invalid or replaced with a space. Several Content-Length values that differ are an unrecoverable error. A Transfer-Encoding whose final coding is not chunked gets 400 and a closed connection. And lenient whitespace handling in the request line is allowed, but the RFC warns it "can result in request smuggling" when recipients interpret robustness differently.

**Case: Akamai, CVE-2025-32094.** Akamai runs one of the largest CDNs, and its edge software is called Ghost. The US National Vulnerability Database (NVD) entry says that before 26 March 2025, an HTTP/1.x OPTIONS request with an `Expect: 100-continue` header (asking the server for a go-ahead before the body is sent; lesson 8 explains it) and **obsolete line folding** could make two in-path Akamai servers interpret the request differently, letting an attacker smuggle a second request in the body. It was classed as CWE-444, fixed across the platform, and disclosed in August 2025 alongside research by James Kettle, director of research at PortSwigger. Three rarely used features (OPTIONS with a body, Expect, obs-fold) had to line up. That is typical: modern desyncs live in the corners of the grammar that real clients never use.

A blocklist (for example, refusing requests that contain the word chunked twice) is not a fix. The space of odd spellings is large and each server normalises differently. The fix is a **strict grammar at every hop**: accept only what the RFC allows, reject everything else with 400, and close the connection.

blocks.question: Parser A trims whitespace around field names; parser B does not. A request contains a Transfer-Encoding field with a space before the colon, plus a Content-Length. If A is the front end and B the back end, which variant is this?
blocks.explain: The front end (A) recognises Transfer-Encoding and frames by chunks; the back end (B) does not recognise it and frames by Content-Length. Front end TE, back end CL: TE.CL.

blocks.question: Which statement best matches RFC 9413's view of the robustness principle?
options: Silently tolerating faulty input causes problems that accumulate; actively maintained protocols should prefer clear, strict handling
blocks.explain: RFC 9413 keeps the parts that protect against defects and attacks but says tolerating unexpected inputs is no longer best practice everywhere, because silent acceptance accumulates interoperability and security debt.

lessons.title: What a desync enables, and what defenders see

blocks.md:
Misplaced bytes become an attack because of *whose* request they land in and *which checks* they skip. RFC 9112 describes request smuggling as hiding "additional requests (which might otherwise be blocked or disabled by policy) within an apparently harmless request". Kettle's 2019 talk at Black Hat USA (a large annual security conference), *HTTP Desync Attacks: Smashing into the Cell Next Door*, showed remote, unauthenticated attackers splicing their requests into other users' requests on commercial and military systems, and used that to redirect victims, poison caches and reach internal APIs (application programming interfaces).

Main consequences:

- **Bypassing front-end controls.** The front end checked only the outer request; the hidden one skipped its access rules and WAF (web application firewall).
- **Corrupting another user's request.** The leftover prefix changes the victim's request, for example its path or headers.
- **Response queue poisoning.** If the back end sees one extra *complete* request, every later response on that connection is handed to the wrong client.

blocks.title: Response queue poisoning at the level of ideas

scenes.caption: The attacker sends one request that, by the back end's framing, contains a second complete request.
The front end sees one request and forwards it. The back end splits it into two: A and B.

add.label: A, read as A then B

scenes.caption: The back end answers both, in order. The front end expected one response, so the answer to B is now waiting in the queue.
The front end passes the first response to the attacker. Then the victim sends an ordinary request on the same back-end connection.
The next response in the queue is B's, so the victim receives it. The response to V, which may carry the victim's private data, is now next in line for whoever asks after.

blocks.md:
**Case: Varnish Cache, CVE-2022-23959.** Varnish is a widely used open-source caching reverse proxy. Its advisory VSV00008 (25 January 2022) said a request smuggling attack could be performed on HTTP/1 connections, and that the smuggled request "would be treated as an additional request by the Varnish server, go through normal VCL processing, and injected as a spurious response on the client connection." VCL is the Varnish Configuration Language. Fixed releases were 6.6.2, 7.0.2 and 6.0.10 LTS (long-term support).

The advisory's detection advice is the general one: smuggled requests "will show in the logs generated by Varnish as normal requests", and may be identified "by comparing the Varnish logs with logs from any proxy software between the Varnish server and the client." In other words, look for places where two tiers disagree about how many requests, or which requests, travelled on a connection.

blocks.caption: Comparing what two tiers logged for each upstream connection. The data is invented for the example.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
c9: front end logged 2, back end 3
c7: unknown method in 'LEFTOVERGET /home HTTP/1.1'
```

Two signals, and you need both. On connection c9 the back end logged one more request than the front end forwarded: a hidden complete request. On c7 the counts match, but the back end saw a request line with a method nobody sends, the fingerprint of a prefix glued onto someone's request. Other signals: bursts of 400 or 405 responses with odd methods, timeouts on otherwise healthy endpoints, and users reporting that they saw someone else's page.

Desync detection is a comparison problem. Log a connection or request identifier at both the front end and the back end, and alert when the request counts or request lines for the same connection differ.

blocks.question: In response queue poisoning, why does the victim receive a response that was not meant for them?
options: The victim's browser cached an old page
The back end answered one more request than the front end forwarded, so every later response on that connection shifts by one
blocks.explain: The front end pairs responses with requests in order. One extra request at the back end produces one extra response, and the pairing is off by one for everyone who follows on that connection.

blocks.question: A front end logs 2 requests on upstream connection c9 and the back end logs 3. What is the most useful next step for a defender?
options: Ignore it; logs are often out of sync
Inspect the extra back-end request and the client request that carried it, and check that tier's parser and desync settings
blocks.explain: A count mismatch on the same connection is the classic signature of a hidden request. The extra entry tells you what was smuggled; the client request before it tells you who sent it and which parsing gap was used.

lessons.title: HTTP/2 framing, and how downgrading brings desync back

blocks.md:
HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) is not text. Each message is carried in binary **frames**, and every frame starts with a fixed 9-byte header whose first field is a 24-bit **Length**. A request is one HEADERS frame (the fields, compressed with **HPACK**, the HTTP/2 header compression format of RFC 7541) followed by zero or more DATA frames; the last frame carries an END_STREAM flag. Request line parts become **pseudo-header fields** whose names start with a colon: `:method`, `:path`, `:scheme` and `:authority` (the host). Browsers and servers agree to use HTTP/2 during the TLS handshake, through the ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) extension, where HTTP/2 over TLS is named h2.

Because every frame states its own length, there is exactly one way to find where a body ends: add up the DATA frames until END_STREAM. That is why HTTP/2 end to end has no CL.TE problem.

The trouble is **downgrading**. Many front ends speak HTTP/2 to browsers but HTTP/1.1 to the back end, rewriting each request as text. Now the HTTP/1.1 framing rules are back, and the front end writes header values that the client chose. RFC 9113 anticipates this:

- A request is **malformed** if its content-length field "does not equal the sum of the DATA frame payload lengths", and intermediaries MUST NOT forward malformed requests.
- Connection-specific fields, including **Transfer-Encoding**, are forbidden; a message carrying them is malformed (only `TE: trailers` is allowed).
- A field value MUST NOT contain CR, LF or NUL, because "failure to validate fields can be exploited for request smuggling attacks" once the message is rewritten as HTTP/1.1, where CR and LF are delimiters.

Skipping the first check gives **H2.CL**; skipping the second gives **H2.TE**; skipping the third lets a client inject whole header lines (CRLF injection).

blocks.caption: A toy downgrade. The HTTP/2 request declares content-length 0 but carries 8 bytes in DATA frames.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
b'POST /a HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s.example\r\ncontent-length: 0\r\n\r\nLEFTOVER'
rejected: malformed: content-length 0 but DATA is 8
```

The naive downgrade writes `content-length: 0` and then the 8 bytes anyway. An HTTP/1.1 back end reads a request with an empty body, and `LEFTOVER` becomes the start of the next request on that connection: an H2.CL desync. The checked downgrade applies RFC 9113 first and rejects the request as malformed, so nothing ambiguous is ever written.

blocks.title: End-to-end HTTP/2 versus a downgrading front end

scenes.caption: The client sends a HEADERS frame and one DATA frame of 8 bytes. The frame header states the length, so the front end knows exactly where the body ends.
Forwarded as HTTP/2, the lengths travel inside the frames. There is no text header for the back end to misread.
Downgraded to HTTP/1.1, the front end copies the client's content-length: 0 into text and appends the 8 body bytes.
A front end that checks content-length against the DATA total, refuses Transfer-Encoding and CR or LF in values never writes the ambiguous text. RFC 9113 requires all three checks.

blocks.md: **Case: Netty, CVE-2021-21295.** Netty is a widely used Java networking framework. Its advisory (March 2021) explained that a content-length in an HTTP/2 request "is not validated by `Http2MultiplexHandler`" as it is passed up. That is harmless for HTTP/2 alone, but if the request is converted into HTTP/1.1 objects and proxied to an HTTP/1.1 peer, "an attacker can smuggle requests inside the body as it gets downgraded". Fixed in 4.1.60.Final; the suggested workaround was a handler that performs the content-length check itself. The same year, Kettle's Black Hat talk *HTTP/2: The Sequel is Always Worse* argued that HTTP/2 cannot be treated as a drop-in transport change with no security impact, and showed HTTP/2-only desyncs against high-profile sites.

HTTP/2 removes framing ambiguity only while the request stays HTTP/2. Every downgrade to HTTP/1.1 must enforce RFC 9113's rules before writing text: content-length equals the DATA total, no connection-specific fields, no CR, LF or NUL in names or values.

blocks.question: A front end accepts HTTP/2 from clients and forwards HTTP/1.1 to the back end. It copies a client's transfer-encoding: chunked field into the rewritten request. What has gone wrong, by RFC 9113?
options: The request was malformed and should have been rejected, because Transfer-Encoding is a connection-specific field
Nothing, Transfer-Encoding is allowed in HTTP/2
The front end should have added a second Transfer-Encoding
The back end should switch to HTTP/3
blocks.explain: RFC 9113 forbids connection-specific fields such as Transfer-Encoding in HTTP/2 and says intermediaries MUST NOT forward malformed requests. Copying it creates the H2.TE variant.

blocks.prompt: An HTTP/2 client sends a header value containing a CR LF pair followed by text that looks like another header. Why is that harmless if the request stays HTTP/2, and dangerous after a careless downgrade?
blocks.reveal: In HTTP/2 the value is a length-delimited string inside an HPACK block: CR and LF are just bytes, not line breaks, though RFC 9113 still says such a request MUST be treated as malformed. After a downgrade the value is written into HTTP/1.1 text, where CR LF *ends a line*, so the bytes after it become a new header line or even a new request. That is why RFC 9113 requires rejecting CR, LF and NUL in field values.

lessons.title: CL.0 and client-side desync: when a server ignores the body

blocks.md:
So far two servers disagreed. A single server can disagree with *itself* if it answers some requests without reading their body. Researchers call this **CL.0**: the sender framed the body with Content-Length, but this server behaves as if Content-Length were 0 on some route, for example a static file, a redirect or an error page. The unread body stays on the connection and becomes the start of the next request.

Why would a server skip the body? Handlers for static files or errors often never look at it, and the server answers immediately. RFC 9112 section 9.3 forbids that shortcut: a server MUST read the entire request message body or close the connection after sending its response, otherwise the remaining data would be misinterpreted as the next request.

blocks.code:
def serve(conn, drain):
    """Answer each request on one keep-alive connection, in order."""
    log = []
    while conn:
        head, _, conn = conn.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
        line = head.split(b"\r\n")[0]
        n = 0
        for h in head.split(b"\r\n")[1:]:
            k, _, v = h.partition(b":")
            if k.lower() == b"content-length":
                n = int(v)
        if line.startswith(b"GET /static/") and not drain:
            pass                     # bug: answered early, body left unread
        else:
            conn = conn[n:]          # consume exactly Content-Length bytes
        log.append(line.decode())
    return log

one = (b"GET /static/logo.png HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s.example\r\n"
       b"Content-Length: 8\r\n\r\nLEFTOVER")
two = b"GET /inbox HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s.example\r\n\r\n"
print("buggy:", serve(one + two, drain=False))
print("fixed:", serve(one + two, drain=True))
blocks.caption: A toy server with one buggy route: requests to /static/ are answered without consuming their body.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
buggy: ['GET /static/logo.png HTTP/1.1', 'LEFTOVERGET /inbox HTTP/1.1']
fixed: ['GET /static/logo.png HTTP/1.1', 'GET /inbox HTTP/1.1']
```

With the bug, the 8-byte body of the first request is never consumed, so the second request is read as `LEFTOVERGET /inbox`. With the fix (consume exactly Content-Length bytes on every route, even ones that ignore the body), the second request is read correctly.

In 2022 Kettle showed why this is worse than it looks, in *Browser-Powered Desync Attacks*. If a server ignores the body, **the victim's own browser** can be the front end. A malicious page makes the browser send a cross-site request with a body to the vulnerable site; the browser then reuses that same connection for the user's next real request to the site, which the server reads with the attacker's prefix. This **client-side desync** needs no proxy at all, so single-server sites and internal networks are exposed. The talk demonstrated it against targets including Apache, Akamai, Varnish, Amazon and several web VPNs (virtual private network portals).

blocks.title: Client-side desync at the level of ideas

scenes.caption: The victim visits the attacker's page. Script on it asks the browser to send a request with a body to the vulnerable site.

add.label: make a request with a body

scenes.caption: The browser opens a connection to the site and sends the request, body included.
The server answers request 1 on a route that ignores the body. The body bytes stay unread on the connection.
The browser reuses the open connection for the user's next request to the site, carrying the user's cookies.
The server reads the leftover body plus request 2 as one request, so the user's own browser delivered the attacker's prefix. Fix: consume the body or close the connection.

blocks.md:
Vendor advisories show the pattern (a third, Cloudflare's, follows below):

- **Apache HTTP Server, CVE-2022-22720** (fixed in 2.4.53, March 2022, credited to James Kettle): the server "fails to close inbound connection when errors are encountered discarding the request body, exposing the server to HTTP Request Smuggling".
- **Cisco ASA (Adaptive Security Appliance) and FTD (Firepower Threat Defense), CVE-2022-20713** (published 10 August 2022, CVSS 4.3, credited to Kettle): a client-side request smuggling flaw in the VPN web client services, letting an attacker who lures a user to a malicious site reflect input into that user's browser. Cisco listed no workaround, only fixed software.

**Cloudflare Pingora, CVE-2025-4366**: in Cloudflare's open-source proxy framework, on a **cache hit** the leftover request body was not consumed, so it could prefix the next request on the same HTTP/1.1 connection. Cloudflare's post-mortem says it was reported through its bug bounty on 11 April 2025 (credited to Kettle and Wannes Verwimp), mitigated by 12 April 06:44 UTC by turning off the affected component, patched, and cached assets were invalidated before traffic returned. Users of the open-source crates (Rust packages) were told to upgrade to Pingora 0.5.0 or later.

Every code path must leave the connection in a known state: either it consumed exactly the declared body, or it closes the connection. Cache hits, redirects, errors and static files are the paths that forget.

blocks.question: Why can a client-side desync affect a site that has no reverse proxy at all?
options: Because the victim's browser reuses its connection to the site, so the browser plays the front end and the site's own unread body bytes prefix the user's next request
blocks.explain: The disagreement is between the browser, which framed the body correctly, and the server, which skipped it. The browser's connection reuse then delivers the leftover bytes ahead of the user's real request.

blocks.question: In the Pingora bug, why did a cache hit matter?
options: The cache stored the request body
On the cache-hit path the proxy answered from cache without consuming the request body, so leftover bytes stayed on the connection
blocks.explain: Normally the body is read or the connection is not reused. The cache-hit shortcut skipped that step, which is exactly the CL.0 pattern in the toy server.

lessons.title: The 2025 endgame: 0.CL, Expect and upstream HTTP/1.1

blocks.md:
By 2025 most big platforms had patched the classic CL.TE and TE.CL patterns. Kettle's 2025 talk, *HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame* (Black Hat USA and DEF CON 33, another large security conference), argued that those mitigations are fragile, presented several new classes of desync that exposed credentials across tech companies, SaaS (software as a service) providers and CDNs, and ended with a call to move the industry beyond HTTP/1.1.

Two ideas from it are worth understanding. **0.CL** is the mirror image of CL.0: the *front end* ignores Content-Length (treats the body as length 0) while the back end honours it. It was long thought unexploitable because it deadlocks: the back end waits for body bytes that the front end never forwards, while the front end waits for a response, until one side times out. The research showed how a back-end route that responds before reading the body breaks the deadlock.

blocks.title: Why 0.CL deadlocks, and what an early response changes

scenes.caption: Illustrative timing, not measured. The front end forwards the headers only; it believes the body is empty.
The back end honours Content-Length and waits for body bytes that will never come. The front end waits for a response.
Both give up at a timeout. Nothing was left on the connection, so there is no desync: this is why 0.CL looked harmless.
If the route answers before reading the body (an early response), the front end moves on and later request bytes are consumed as this body: the boundary has moved again.

blocks.md: The second idea is **Expect-based desync**. RFC 9110 defines `Expect: 100-continue`: the client sends headers first and waits for a 100 (Continue) interim response before sending a possibly large body. That splits one request into two phases, and proxies handle the phases inconsistently, for example when they do not honour the header, or receive an early final response instead of 100. The Akamai bug in lesson 4 was one of these. Fastly, another CDN, published a statement in August 2025 that it was not vulnerable to the new vectors, crediting a single parsing implementation across its stack, rejecting ambiguous HTTP/1.1 requests "immediately, before any processing begins", rejecting malformed Expect headers, and reconstructing requests before forwarding.

**The argument against upstream HTTP/1.1.** PortSwigger's write-up for security leaders summarises the conclusion: patching individual parsers will not end the class, so move internal and upstream connections to HTTP/2, where each frame carries its length, and ask vendors whether they support upstream HTTP/2 and when. It also warns that systems which advertise HTTP/2 to clients but use HTTP/1.1 internally are especially risky, and that regex filters mostly hide the problem.

Support is arriving: nginx's documentation now lists `proxy_http_version 2` for proxied connections (since nginx 1.29.4, requiring its HTTP/2 module), next to 1.0 and 1.1.

blocks.caption: Illustrative nginx configuration, not run here: certificates and other required settings are omitted. Check the version you run supports the directive value before relying on it.

blocks.md: The structural fix for request smuggling is to stop sending HTTP/1.1 between your own servers. Until then, every hop must reject ambiguous requests, and every code path must consume the body or close the connection.

blocks.question: What distinguishes a 0.CL desync from a CL.0 desync?
options: 0.CL: the front end ignores Content-Length while the back end honours it. CL.0: the front end honours it while the back end ignores it
They are two names for the same thing
blocks.explain: The notation is front end first. In 0.CL the back end waits for body bytes the front end never forwarded; in CL.0 the back end leaves forwarded body bytes unread.

blocks.question: Why did researchers long consider 0.CL unexploitable?
options: It needs a valid TLS certificate
Front end and back end wait on each other until a timeout, so no bytes end up misplaced
blocks.explain: The back end waits for a body that never arrives while the front end waits for a response. A timeout ends the exchange cleanly unless some route answers early, which is what the 2025 research found.

lessons.title: Defending a proxy chain: normalise, reject, close, upgrade

blocks.md:
Put the defences in order of strength:

1. **HTTP/2 end to end**, including the hop from your proxy to the origin, so no hop ever parses HTTP/1.1 framing.
2. If a hop must speak HTTP/1.1: the **front end normalises** each request (one framing header, clean field names, no obs-fold) and **rejects** anything it cannot normalise with 400 and a closed connection.
3. The **back end rejects** ambiguous requests too, in case the front end has a bug.
4. **Consume the body or close the connection** on every code path, especially early responses.
5. Where you cannot trust parsing, **disable back-end connection reuse**. It removes the shared stream at a cost in latency and load.
6. **Reject bodies on GET, HEAD and OPTIONS**, which legitimate clients rarely send. The 2025 research recommends this; the Akamai bug in lesson 4, for example, needed an OPTIONS request with a body.

A WAF in front does not substitute for these: Kettle's 2025 work warns against relying on WAFs, and RFC 9112 puts the burden on each recipient's parser.

**A managed example: AWS Application Load Balancer.** AWS (Amazon Web Services) built an open-source Rust library, [HTTP Desync Guardian](https://github.com/aws/http-desync-guardian), that classifies each request, and its Application Load Balancer exposes it as **desync mitigation mode**. Requests are classed as **Compliant** (complies with RFC 7230, the older HTTP/1.1 spec, and poses no known threat), **Acceptable** (not compliant, no known threat), **Ambiguous** (not compliant, and "various web servers and proxies could handle it differently") or **Severe** (high risk: blocked with a 400 and the client connection closed). Three modes decide what happens: **monitor**, **defensive** (the default) and **strictest**. In defensive mode, Ambiguous requests are routed but both the client and target connections are closed afterwards, so leftover bytes cannot reach another request.

blocks.title: AWS ALB desync mitigation: what each mode does

scenes.caption: 1 means allowed, 0.5 allowed but both connections closed afterwards, 0 blocked. Values from the AWS documentation table.
Monitor mode only records the classification; every class is allowed. Useful for a first look at your traffic, not for protection.
Defensive (the default) blocks Severe requests and closes connections after Ambiguous ones, so they cannot desync a reused connection.
Strictest blocks everything that is not Compliant. Safest, but legitimate odd clients may break; AWS notes the availability trade-off.

blocks.code:
# Inspect, then harden, an AWS Application Load Balancer
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn "$ALB_ARN"

aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn "$ALB_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=routing.http.desync_mitigation_mode,Value=strictest \
               Key=routing.http.drop_invalid_header_fields.enabled,Value=true
blocks.caption: Names from the AWS ALB docs; $ALB_ARN is its ARN (Amazon Resource Name). drop_invalid_header_fields removes header fields whose names do not match [-A-Za-z0-9]+ instead of forwarding them. Run monitor mode first and read the classifications to see what strictest would block.

blocks.md: The load balancer also tells you *why*. Each [access log](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-access-logs.html) line records the classification and a `classification_reason`, and the metric in CloudWatch (AWS's monitoring service) `DesyncMitigationMode_NonCompliant_Request_Count` counts non-compliant requests. Reason codes map straight onto this course: `BothTeClPresent` (both framing headers, Ambiguous), `MultipleContentLength` (different values, Severe), `DuplicateContentLength` (same value repeated, Ambiguous), `BadTransferEncoding` (Severe), `SuspiciousHeader` (a field that "can be normalized to Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length using common text normalization techniques", Ambiguous), `BadHeader` (null or carriage return in a header, Severe) and `UndefinedContentLengthSemantics` (Content-Length on a GET or HEAD, Ambiguous).

**Configuration can create smuggling too.** Apache HTTP Server's CVE-2023-25690 (versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.55, fixed in 2.4.56, March 2023, found by Lars Krapf of Adobe) affected `mod_proxy` (Apache's reverse-proxy module) setups where a `RewriteRule` (from mod_rewrite, which rewrites URLs by pattern) or `ProxyPassMatch` matched part of the user's URL with a non-specific pattern and pasted it into the proxied request target. Request splitting could then bypass proxy access controls, reach unintended URLs and poison caches. The vulnerable shape, from the advisory, is below; the fix is upgrading, and the design lesson is to avoid re-inserting raw user input into a request line you build.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable shape quoted in the Apache advisory for CVE-2023-25690
# (affects 2.4.0 to 2.4.55): user path data is captured by (.*)
# and substituted into the proxied request target.
RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule "^/here/(.*)" "http://example.com:8080/elsewhere?$1" [P]
ProxyPassReverse /here/ http://example.com:8080/

# Fix: upgrade to 2.4.56 or later. Where you can, proxy a fixed
# prefix instead of rebuilding the target from captured user input:
ProxyPass        /here/ http://example.com:8080/elsewhere/
ProxyPassReverse /here/ http://example.com:8080/elsewhere/
blocks.caption: The first block is quoted from the Apache advisory. The ProxyPass alternative is a general hardening choice, not part of the advisory, and still requires a patched server.

blocks.question: Your ALB runs in defensive mode and logs many requests with classification_reason BothTeClPresent. What is the load balancer doing with them?
options: Routing them, then closing both the client and target connections so leftover bytes cannot reach another request
blocks.explain: BothTeClPresent is classed Ambiguous. In defensive mode Ambiguous requests are routed but the connections are closed afterwards. Strictest mode would block them.

blocks.question: Which single change removes HTTP/1.1 framing ambiguity between your CDN and your origin?
options: Switching the CDN-to-origin hop to HTTP/2
blocks.explain: With HTTP/2 on that hop, every frame carries its own length and RFC 9113 rules apply; there is no Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding choice left to disagree about. WAF rules can only recognise known bad shapes.

lessons.title: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary

blocks.md:
Now the second family of bugs. A **cache** stores responses so later requests can be answered without asking the origin. A **private cache** belongs to one user (the browser's cache); a **shared cache** serves many users (a CDN edge, a reverse proxy such as Varnish or nginx). Only shared caches can turn one user's request into everyone's response, so this course is about them.

RFC 9111, the HTTP caching standard, defines the **cache key**: "the information a cache uses to choose a response", composed "at a minimum" of the request method and target URI. In practice many caches key on host plus path plus query string. nginx's default key, for example, is `$scheme$proxy_host$request_uri`. Everything *not* in the key is assumed not to matter: two requests with the same key get the same stored response.

When may a shared cache store a response? RFC 9111 section 3 says it MUST NOT store one if the response has `Cache-Control: no-store`, or `private` (meant for a single user), or if the request carried an `Authorization` header (unless the response explicitly allows it). Otherwise it needs a reason to store: `public`, `max-age=N` (fresh for N seconds), `s-maxage=N` (shared caches only), an `Expires` time, or a status code defined as **heuristically cacheable**. RFC 9110 lists 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414 and 501; for these a cache may guess a freshness lifetime.

Two traps follow. RFC 9111 notes that `Set-Cookie` does **not** stop caching: a cacheable response with a cookie "can be (and often is)" served to others, unless Cache-Control says otherwise. And caches can be configured to override the origin, for example nginx's `proxy_ignore_headers Cache-Control` or a CDN rule that caches by file extension.

blocks.title: A cache miss, a hit, and a private page

scenes.caption: Ana requests /logo.png. The cache has nothing under that key: a MISS, so it asks the origin.
The origin says the response is public and fresh for 300 seconds. The cache stores it under the key and returns it.
Ben asks for /logo.png within 300 seconds. Same key, so the cache answers itself: a HIT. The origin never sees Ben's request.
Ana loads /account. The origin marks it no-store, private, so a correct shared cache forwards it every time and never stores it.

blocks.md:
**Vary** handles the case where the response legitimately depends on a request header. RFC 9110 says the Vary response field lists the parts of the request, "aside from the method and target URI", that might have influenced the response, for example `Vary: Accept-Language`. RFC 9111 then forbids reusing a stored response unless those listed request fields match. In effect, Vary adds the named headers to the key. nginx honours it, and does not cache `Vary: *` at all.

Caches announce their decisions in response headers that differ by product: many add an `X-Cache: HIT` or `MISS` style header, and the standard `Age` header says how many seconds a response has spent in caches. Defenders use these to check which pages are being stored.

A cache key is a promise: "any two requests with this key deserve the same response". Every attack in the next lessons breaks that promise, either because the response depended on something outside the key, or because two different resources ended up under one key.

blocks.question: Which response may a shared cache store, following RFC 9111?
options: Any response to a request that carried an Authorization header, by default
200 with Cache-Control: max-age=600 and no other restrictions
blocks.explain: max-age gives explicit freshness and nothing forbids shared storage. private and no-store forbid it, and a request with Authorization may not be stored by a shared cache unless the response explicitly allows it.

blocks.question: A login response sets a session cookie with Set-Cookie and has Cache-Control: public, max-age=60. What does RFC 9111 say about Set-Cookie here?
options: Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching; this response could be stored and served to others
Set-Cookie is stripped by every cache
blocks.explain: RFC 9111 section 7.3 says Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching. Some caches (nginx by default) refuse to store such responses, but you cannot rely on that; the origin must send no-store or private.

lessons.title: Web cache poisoning: inputs that change the page but not the key

blocks.md:
**Web cache poisoning** means getting a harmful response stored under a key that ordinary visitors use. RFC 9111 warns that storing malicious content "can extend the reach of an attacker to affect multiple users".

The enabling bug is an **unkeyed input**: something in the request that changes the response but is not part of the cache key. A common one is **X-Forwarded-Host**, a de facto header (widely used, never standardised) that proxies add to tell the application which host the client originally asked for. Applications use it to build absolute URLs. If a cache sits in front, keys only on host and path, and the application trusts X-Forwarded-Host from anyone, then whoever sends the header first decides what every later visitor gets.

blocks.caption: A toy origin that reflects X-Forwarded-Host into a script URL, behind a toy shared cache. attacker.example is a reserved example domain.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
vulnerable attacker MISS <script src="https://attacker.example/app.js"></script>
vulnerable victim   HIT  <script src="https://attacker.example/app.js"></script>
keyed      attacker MISS <script src="https://attacker.example/app.js"></script>
keyed      victim   MISS <script src="https://shop.example/app.js"></script>
fixed app  attacker MISS <script src="https://shop.example/app.js"></script>
fixed app  victim   HIT  <script src="https://shop.example/app.js"></script>
```

In the vulnerable setup, the first request stores a page whose script comes from another host, and the victim's ordinary request is a HIT on that stored page. Adding the header to the cache key (or listing it in `Vary`) stops the victim sharing the entry, but the cleaner fix is in the application: it builds URLs from a configured canonical host and ignores client-supplied forwarding headers, so the input no longer changes the response at all.

scenes.caption: The attacker requests the home page with an extra forwarding header. The cache key is only host and path, so this request has the same key as everyone's.
MISS: the cache forwards. The origin trusts the header and builds its script URL from it.
Any visitor requesting / in the next 300 seconds gets the stored page, which loads script from a host the attacker chose.
With the fix, the origin ignores the client's header and always uses its canonical host, so the stored page is correct whoever filled the cache.

blocks.md: **Case: Practical Web Cache Poisoning (2018).** Kettle's Black Hat USA 2018 talk, [*Practical Web Cache Poisoning: Redefining 'Unexploitable'*](https://infocondb.org/con/black-hat/black-hat-usa-2018/practical-web-cache-poisoning-redefining-unexploitable), showed that adding a cache in front of a site can turn it critically vulnerable, with exploit chains that hijacked JavaScript and crossed cache layers. As reported by TechTarget, Kettle used an extension Kettle had built for Burp Suite, **Param Miner**, which finds unkeyed inputs, and changed X-Forwarded-Host on the Red Hat home page to get Kettle's own content cached for its visitors. The research also reached infrastructure behind Firefox's **Shield** feature, which fetches update recipes; Mozilla signed the recipes, so Kettle could not push new code, but could replay an old recipe for a vulnerable extension. Mozilla patched within 24 hours and paid a USD 1,000 bounty after a disagreement about severity.

**Defender checklist for poisoning.**

- Know your key: list exactly which request parts your CDN and proxies key on.
- Make the origin deterministic from keyed inputs: do not let headers such as X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme or custom debug headers change cacheable responses. If a proxy must send them, have the edge overwrite or strip whatever the client sent.
- Unkeyed inputs are not only headers: caches often drop some query parameters (for example tracking parameters) from the key, so the origin must ignore those too.
- If a response truly depends on a header, say so with `Vary`, and accept the lower hit rate.
- Cache HTML conservatively; static assets are the safe default for long caching.
- Detect: periodically fetch key pages through the cache and directly from the origin and compare; alert on cached pages referencing unexpected hosts. Respond by fixing the origin, then **purging** the poisoned entries, since the fix does not remove what is already stored.

blocks.question: A cache keys on host and path. The origin adds the value of a client-supplied header into the page. What does this make the header?
options: An unkeyed input, the precondition for cache poisoning
A hop-by-hop header that never reaches the origin
blocks.explain: The header changes the response but not the key, so whoever sends it first decides what everyone with that key receives.

blocks.question: You fix the origin so it ignores X-Forwarded-Host. Users still receive the bad page for a few minutes. Why, and what do you do?
options: The fix failed; roll it back
The poisoned response is still stored until it expires; purge the affected cache entries
blocks.explain: Fixing the origin stops new poisoning but does not touch responses already stored. Purge the entries (or wait out max-age) and confirm with a fresh fetch through the cache.

lessons.title: Poisoning with errors and with normalisation

blocks.md: A poisoned entry does not have to contain an attack. It can simply be an **error**. In 2019 Hoai Viet Nguyen, Luigi Lo Iacono and Hannes Federrath presented **CPDoS** (cache-poisoned denial of service) at ACM CCS (the Association for Computing Machinery's Conference on Computer and Communications Security). The idea: send a request that the cache accepts and forwards, but that makes the origin return an error; if the cache stores the error under the normal key, every visitor gets the error. Their three variants are below.

- **HHO** (HTTP header oversize): the cache allows larger request headers than the origin, so the origin answers 400.
- **HMC** (HTTP meta character): a header contains control characters such as line feed or carriage return, which the cache forwards and the origin rejects.
- **HMO** (HTTP method override): a header such as X-HTTP-Method-Override makes the application treat a GET as another method, and the resulting error is cached for the GET.

They tested fifteen web caching solutions and found one proxy cache product and five CDN services vulnerable, as [The Hacker News reported](https://thehackernews.com/2019/10/cdn-cache-poisoning-dos-attack.html). AWS responded by no longer caching 400 Bad Request pages by default on CloudFront.

blocks.caption: A toy cache that stores any status, next to one that stores only the status codes RFC 9110 lists as heuristically cacheable. The header sizes are illustrative.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
caches every status  first: ('MISS', (400, 'Bad Request'))  everyone after: ('HIT ', (400, 'Bad Request'))
caches RFC set only  first: ('MISS', (400, 'Bad Request'))  everyone after: ('MISS', (200, 'the real home page'))
```

One oversized request is enough to put the 400 in the vulnerable cache, and every later visitor gets it. The fixed cache never stores the 400, because 400 is not on RFC 9110's heuristic list, so the next visitor's request reaches the origin and gets the real page. (Simplified: an explicit cache rule could still store a 400; the point is to never configure one.)

blocks.title: Next 5 visitors after one bad request

scenes.caption: Counts from running the toy with five ordinary visitors after the attacker's single request. The cache that stores any status serves the error to all five. The other cache is shown next.
The cache that stores only heuristically cacheable codes serves the real page to all five. The error reached only the request that caused it.

blocks.md: **Fixes for CPDoS.** Do not cache error responses unless you mean to, and if you do, keep them short-lived; send `Cache-Control: no-store` on error pages. Make the cache's limits no looser than the origin's (header size, allowed characters), so the cache rejects first. Use the precise status: [RFC 6585](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585.html) defines **431 Request Header Fields Too Large** for oversized headers, and says caches MUST NOT store 431 responses. And do not honour method-override headers on GET.

**Cache key normalisation** is the other side of the same coin. Caches often *normalise* the key, for example decoding percent-encoded characters or removing parts of the path, while the origin interprets the raw URL. If the cache maps two different URLs to one key but the origin serves different content for them, an attacker can fill the shared key with the wrong resource. Martin Doyhenard of PortSwigger presented this as **Cache Key Confusion** at [DEF CON 32 (2024)](https://infocondb.org/con/def-con/def-con-32/gotta-cache-em-all-bending-the-rules-of-web-cache-exploitation), exploiting URL parsing inconsistencies in major platforms including Microsoft Azure, to the point of arbitrary cache poisoning and full denial of service.

Cache and origin must agree on two things: which requests are errors, and which URLs are the same resource. Make the cache stricter than the origin on input, and make its key normalisation match how the origin routes.

blocks.question: Why does caching a 400 response turn one malformed request into a denial of service?
options: The error is stored under the normal key, so every later visitor receives the error instead of the page
blocks.explain: The origin is fine; the cache is now answering everyone with the stored error until it expires or is purged.

blocks.question: A cache decodes percent-encoding in paths before building its key; the origin does not decode before routing. What can go wrong?
options: Two URLs the origin treats as different resources can share one cache key, so one resource's response is served for the other
blocks.explain: The cache believes the two requests are the same; the origin does not. Whichever response is stored first is served for both: a cache key confusion.

lessons.title: Web cache deception: making the cache keep a private page

blocks.md:
Poisoning pushes the attacker's content to victims. **Web cache deception** runs the other way: it tricks the cache into storing the *victim's* private response somewhere the attacker can read it.

Omer Gil, then an information security team leader at EY's (Ernst & Young's) Advanced Security Center, presented it at [Black Hat USA 2017](https://infocondb.org/con/black-hat/black-hat-usa-2017/web-cache-deception-attack). Gil's whitepaper asks what happens with a URL like `/home.php/nonexistent.css`, where `home.php` is a real page. Many servers ignore the extra path and return `home.php`'s content, with its `text/html` type. A cache that decides by **file extension** sees `.css`, assumes a public stylesheet, and stores the page. Gil listed three conditions: the server returns the page's content for such a URL; the cache stores files by extension, "disregarding any caching headers"; and the victim is logged in when they open the URL. The USENIX Security 2020 paper on the topic notes that Gil demonstrated it against PayPal, leaking details of a private payment account.

blocks.title: Web cache deception step by step

scenes.caption: The attacker sends the victim a link to their own account page with a fake stylesheet name appended.
The victim's browser requests it with their session cookie. The cache has nothing stored for this path, so it forwards.
The origin's route matches the /account prefix, ignores the rest and returns the victim's private page.
The cache sees .css, ignores the headers and stores the page under /account/x.css, then returns it to the victim, who notices nothing.
The attacker requests the same URL without any cookie and receives the stored private page: a HIT.

blocks.caption: Toy origin and cache. The origin either matches routes by prefix or exactly, and drops anything after a semicolon. The cache stores 200 responses whose path ends in .css, .js or .png, optionally honouring Cache-Control.

blocks.prompt: Before reading the output: exact routing will clearly stop `/account/x.css` (the origin returns 404). Will exact routing also stop `/account;x.css`? Which of the three setups stops both URLs?
blocks.reveal: Exact routing does not stop `/account;x.css`. The cache and the origin split that path differently: the cache sees the whole string ending in `.css`, while the origin treats `;` as the start of parameters and routes on `/account` alone, an exact match. Exact routing fixed the origin's matching rule but not the disagreement about where the path ends. Only the cache honouring the origin's `no-store, private` stops both, because it no longer depends on how anyone parses the path.

blocks.md:
Output:
```
/account/x.css  prefix route, ignores headers attacker gets HIT  200 balance of victim: 1,204
/account/x.css  exact route                   attacker gets MISS 404 not found
/account/x.css  honours Cache-Control         attacker gets MISS 302 log in first
/account;x.css  prefix route, ignores headers attacker gets HIT  200 balance of victim: 1,204
/account;x.css  exact route                   attacker gets HIT  200 balance of victim: 1,204
/account;x.css  honours Cache-Control         attacker gets MISS 302 log in first
```

For `/account/x.css`, an **exact** route returns 404, which removes Gil's first condition. But look at `/account;x.css`: the origin strips everything after the semicolon (some frameworks treat it as path parameters) and still serves the account page, so exact routing alone fails. Only **honouring Cache-Control** fixes both URLs: the origin already said `no-store, private`, and a cache that listens never stores the page. The next lesson looks at these delimiter differences.

blocks.caption: nginx configuration, not run here. Directives are from the nginx proxy module documentation: header-set caching parameters take priority over proxy_cache_valid, and responses with Set-Cookie are not cached unless proxy_ignore_headers says otherwise.

blocks.md: Gil's whitepaper gives four mitigations: cache files only if their HTTP caching headers allow it; keep static files in a dedicated directory and cache only that; cache by **content type** where the cache supports it; and make the server return 404 or 302 for URLs such as `/home.php/nonexistent.css` instead of the page. [Cloudflare's April 2017 response](https://blog.cloudflare.com/understanding-our-cache-and-the-web-cache-deception-attack/) told customers to make sure the origin never treats a nonexistent path as its parent, and explained that an origin `no-store` or `private` keeps a response out of its cache unless a Cache Everything rule with an Edge Cache TTL overrides it. It later added **Cache Deception Armor**, which checks that a URL's extension matches the response's Content-Type and does not cache on a mismatch (an HTML page served for `.jpg` is not cached).

Defence in depth matters here because the origin and the cache are often owned by different teams. The origin team should mark every personalised response `Cache-Control: no-store, private`; the CDN team should make sure no rule overrides that. Either alone has been bypassed in practice.

blocks.question: Which single condition, if removed, stops the classic web cache deception attack even if the origin keeps returning the page for /account/x.css?
options: The cache storing by file extension while ignoring the origin's Cache-Control: no-store, private
The attacker knowing the victim's email
blocks.explain: If the cache respects the origin's no-store or private, the private page is never stored, whatever the URL looks like. HTTPS protects the network hop, not what the cache keeps.

lessons.title: Path confusion at scale: delimiters, studies and ChatGPT 2023

blocks.md: Web cache deception is a special case of **path confusion**: the cache and the origin disagree about what a URL path means. *Cached and Confused: Web Cache Deception in the Wild* (USENIX Security Symposium 2020, by Seyed Ali Mirheidari, Sajjad Arshad, Kaan Onarlioglu, Bruno Crispo, Engin Kirda and William Robertson) measured it on high-profile sites from the Alexa top 5,000 (a website popularity ranking): 295 sites in a first experiment and 340 in a follow-up that tried path variations. In the first, 16 of the 295 sites were vulnerable; 14 of those 16 leaked personal data such as names, usernames, email addresses and phone numbers, 6 leaked CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tokens and 6 leaked session identifiers or user-specific API tokens. They found many popular sites "remain vulnerable two years after the public disclosure", that the presence of cache headers was an unreliable indicator of whether a page was cached, and concluded that "web caches are not plug & play technologies".

The paper also generalised the trick beyond `/page/x.css`. Its variations replace the slash with characters that the **origin** treats as the end of the path but the **cache** does not: an encoded newline, an encoded semicolon, an encoded `#` or an encoded `?`. Whether each works depends on the exact pair of parsers, which is the whole point: a URL has no single correct reading across all software.

In 2024 Martin Doyhenard extended this in *Gotta Cache 'em All* (DEF CON 32) with **Static Path Deception**, abusing cache rules for static *directories* rather than extensions, and showed a case study of nginx behind Cloudflare. That is why the static-directory rule from the last lesson is only safe together with its other half: the cache still honours the origin's `no-store, private`.

scenes.caption: One path reaches two parsers with different ideas of where the path ends.
The cache reads the whole string and applies its static-file rule because it ends in .css.
The origin stops at the semicolon and serves /account, the logged-in user's private page.
Put together, the private page is stored as if it were a public stylesheet.
If the cache honours the origin's no-store, private, the disagreement about the path no longer matters: nothing is stored.

blocks.md: **Case: ChatGPT, March 2023.** Gal Nagli, a bug bounty hunter and founder of the security company Shockwave, reported a web cache deception flaw in ChatGPT: an attacker could craft a link adding a `.css` path to the session endpoint, and if a logged-in victim opened it, the cached response exposed the victim's name, email and **access token**, enough for account takeover. OpenAI's first fix told the caching server not to cache that endpoint, matching it with a regex (regular expression). Security researcher Ayoub Fathi then found a bypass affecting other ChatGPT API endpoints that could expose conversation titles, full chats and account status, and OpenAI fixed that too. Neither researcher was paid, because OpenAI had no bug bounty programme at the time, as [SecurityWeek reported](https://www.securityweek.com/openai-patches-account-takeover-vulnerabilities-in-chatgpt/) on 29 March 2023.

The ChatGPT sequence is the lesson in miniature. The first fix was a **deny-list** in the cache (do not cache this one endpoint), which left every similar endpoint and every other path spelling open. The durable fix is the opposite direction: the cache stores only what the origin marks cacheable, and every authenticated API response carries `Cache-Control: no-store, private`. Tokens that may have been exposed must be revoked, because purging the cache does not un-leak them.

Never let the cache infer cacheability from what the URL looks like. Let the origin declare it with Cache-Control, make the cache honour it, and cache by allow-list (a static directory, matching Content-Type) rather than by deny-list.

blocks.question: Why was a regex rule excluding one ChatGPT endpoint from caching not a complete fix?
options: It was a deny-list for one path; other endpoints and path spellings were still cached by the extension rule
blocks.explain: The bypass reached other API endpoints. A deny-list has to anticipate every path the cache might misread; an allow-list plus origin Cache-Control does not.

blocks.question: In the USENIX 2020 study, what did the authors find about cache headers?
options: They always reveal whether a page was cached
Their presence was an unreliable indicator of whether a resource is cached, so tools relying on them can miss vulnerabilities
blocks.explain: The paper reports that the presence of cache headers was an unreliable indicator, implying that detection tools relying on that signal may produce false negatives.

blocks.md:
Pull the course together as a defender's runbook.

**Prevent (desync).** HTTP/2 on every hop you control; strict parsing with 400 and close on every HTTP/1.1 hop; consume the body or close on every code path; no bodies on GET, HEAD or OPTIONS; managed modes such as ALB defensive or strictest.

**Prevent (caches).** Know the key; keep cacheable responses deterministic from keyed inputs; `Cache-Control: no-store, private` on every personalised response; caches that honour origin headers and cache by allow-list; no cached errors; matching normalisation between cache and origin.

**Detect.** Per-connection request counts and request lines compared across tiers; unknown methods and odd request lines in back-end logs; ALB `classification_reason` and the non-compliant request metric; cached pages fetched through the edge compared with the origin; cache hits on paths that should never be cached, such as account or API paths.

blocks.code:
# What to look for, per log source (illustrative field names vary)
front-end / back-end access logs:
  same upstream connection, different request counts     : hidden request
  request line with an unknown method or glued prefix    : leftover bytes
  400 or 405 bursts from one client, odd framing headers : probing
load balancer (AWS ALB):
  classification = Ambiguous | Severe, classification_reason = BothTeClPresent ...
  CloudWatch DesyncMitigationMode_NonCompliant_Request_Count rising
CDN / cache logs:
  HIT on /account, /api, /session paths                    : deception
  cached HTML that references an unexpected host           : poisoning
  cached 4xx or 5xx on popular keys                         : CPDoS
blocks.caption: A checklist, not a parser. Map each line onto your own log fields.

blocks.title: Responding to a desync or cache incident

nodes.label:
Detect
log mismatch or bad HIT

scenes.caption: A comparison alert or an unexpected cache HIT opens the incident.
Contain first: switch to the strictest parsing mode you can tolerate and turn off back-end connection reuse. Cloudflare's Pingora response disabled the affected component within a day of the report.
Fix the root cause: patch the parser, remove the overriding cache rule, add Cache-Control: no-store, private to personalised responses.
Purge what is already stored: fixes do not remove poisoned or private entries. Cloudflare invalidated cached assets before re-enabling traffic.
Revoke anything that may have leaked (sessions, access tokens), then add a regression test, such as the toy parser pairs in this course, so the gap cannot return.

blocks.md: **A safe way to practise: differential testing on your own code.** Every toy in this course is the same harness: feed one input to two parsers and compare their decisions. Build that into your test suite for your own proxy and application: generate odd but well-defined inputs (duplicate fields, whitespace around names, folded lines, unusual chunk sizes, paths with `;`, encoded characters and static-looking suffixes) and assert that every tier either rejects the input or agrees with every other tier. Run it against servers you own, on localhost or in a lab network.

**Legal practice.** The [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security) has free, deliberately vulnerable labs on request smuggling, web cache poisoning and web cache deception, run on PortSwigger's own infrastructure for exactly this purpose. [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF) offers free capture-the-flag challenges. [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/), from OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project), is an intentionally insecure web app you can run locally to practise web testing in general.

Keep to the line from the start of the course: on real sites, these bugs affect *other* users' requests and cached pages, so test only systems you own or are explicitly authorised to test, and stop at proving the parsing difference.

Desync and cache attacks are the same lesson twice: when two components interpret one message differently, an attacker chooses the difference. Remove ambiguity (HTTP/2 upstream, strict parsing, origin-declared caching), detect disagreement by comparing tiers, and clean up stored state after every fix.

blocks.question: After fixing a web cache deception bug, why must you also revoke sessions or tokens?
options: Responses already stored or fetched may have exposed tokens; purging the cache does not invalidate copies an attacker already holds
It is needed to enable HTTP/2
blocks.explain: The fix and the purge stop future exposure. Anything already read by an attacker, such as the access tokens in the ChatGPT case, stays valid until revoked.

blocks.question: Which test best catches a new desync before deployment?
options: A load test with normal traffic
Checking that the home page returns 200
A differential test that sends odd but well-defined requests through every tier you own and checks that all tiers reject or agree
blocks.explain: Desyncs appear only on unusual inputs and only as disagreements. Normal traffic and status checks pass on a vulnerable stack; comparing tiers on edge-case inputs is what reveals the gap.
